title: Why We Put Things Off
focus: Second conditional and advice (If I were you, I'd ...)

lines.text: Welcome to Better Days. Today's topic is something we all do: putting things off.
Guilty. I've been meaning to clean my garage for two years.
Why do we do it? It's not just laziness, is it?
Not at all. Psychologists say that we often avoid tasks because they make us feel uncomfortable, not because we're lazy.
So the problem is emotional?
In many cases, yes. If the task felt pleasant, you'd start immediately.
What practical advice is there?
If I were you, I'd break the task into very small steps. Instead of cleaning the garage, say you'll clear one shelf.
That sounds easy.
It is, and that's the point. Once you've started, continuing is far less painful.
What about deadlines?
Set your own earlier ones, and tell a friend. If someone's expecting your result, you're much more likely to deliver it.
Would you say rewards help?
Definitely. If you finish the shelf, treat yourself to a coffee. Small rewards keep you going.

title: Saturday at the Market
focus: Time clauses and future (as soon as, until, by the time, once, as long as)

lines.text: It's eight o'clock on a Saturday morning, and the market is already full. I'm here with a cheese seller, Mr Bell.
Good morning. I'll be here until two, or until I've sold everything, whichever comes first.
When do you start preparing?
By the time most people wake up, I've been working for hours. I leave home at four.
Why do customers prefer markets to supermarkets?
Many say they like knowing where their food comes from. As soon as they taste a sample, they usually buy.
Do prices stay low?
Not always. Once you add transport and fuel costs, cheese from a small farm can't compete with big shops.
So how do you survive?
Quality. Customers will keep coming back as long as the cheese is good.
Has the market changed over the years?
Definitely. When I started, there were only six stalls. By the end of this year, there'll be over forty.
That's a big change. Any worries?
Rent for the stalls is going up, so I'll have to raise prices unless the council helps us.
Let's hope it does. Thank you, Mr Bell.

title: A Difficult Conversation
focus: Softening criticism (I wonder if, it might be better to, I'd have thought)

lines.text: Callum, do you have a minute? I'd like to talk about the client presentation.
Of course. I thought it went rather well.
Parts of it did. Your slides were clear, and the client liked the timeline. I wonder, though, if we could talk about the time spent on the budget section.
You mean it was too long?
It might have been a little long. I noticed that Mr Peters started checking his phone.
Hmm. I wanted to be thorough, because he'd asked about costs by email.
I understand, and that's a good instinct. It might be better to give the main numbers first, and keep the detail in a handout.
That makes sense. I hadn't thought about a handout.
Also, I'd have thought you'd have invited questions earlier. People tend to engage more when they can interrupt.
I was worried I'd lose my place, to be honest.
That's quite common. Maybe try writing the questions you expect on a card?
I'll do that. Thanks for being straightforward, but kind.
You did a lot well, Callum. This is just polishing.

title: Between Two Languages
focus: Ability and achievement (manage to, be able to, succeed in)

lines.text: Daniel, you work as a conference interpreter. Is it as stressful as it looks?
Sometimes more. I have to listen and speak at the same moment, so my brain is working very hard.
How long can you keep it up?
About half an hour. After that, we swap with a colleague, otherwise the quality drops.
Were you able to speak both languages from childhood?
One of them. I grew up speaking Portuguese at home, and I managed to reach a high level of English through years of study abroad.
What if you don't know a word?
You can't stop. You find another way to say it. Succeeding in this job means accepting that you can't be perfect.
Have you ever made a serious mistake?
Once, I gave a wrong figure in a business meeting. Luckily, I managed to correct it within seconds.
What's the best preparation?
Reading about the topic beforehand. I wasn't able to follow a medical talk once, and I promised myself never again.
Do you ever feel invisible?
Often, and I like it. If people notice me, I'm probably not doing my job well.

title: Roll the Dice

lines.text: Welcome to Weekend Plans. Today: board game cafes, which have become surprisingly popular.
I do love them. I went to one last Friday and stayed for four hours.
Four hours? What do you actually do there?
You pay a small fee, choose from hundreds of games, and somebody explains the rules. That last part does help, because some games are complicated.
Is it mainly young people?
You'd think so, but no. Last week I did see a group of grandparents playing with their grandchildren.
Why do you think they're successful?
People are tired of screens. A table, a game and a few friends are all you need.
Do games get too competitive?
They do sometimes! I once watched two friends argue for ten minutes about a scoring mistake.
How did it end?
They did make up eventually, after buying each other a hot chocolate.
Any recommendation for beginners?
Start with a cooperative game, where everyone wins or loses together. It does remove the pressure.

title: Why Parks Matter
focus: Describing trends (rise, fall, remain stable) and cause versus correlation

lines.text: Good morning. Today I'd like to look at how urban green spaces affect the people who live near them.
Researchers in many countries have noticed a similar pattern. People who live near parks tend to report lower stress.
Imagine a survey in which half of residents say they visit a park every week. Five years later, after new paths and benches are added, that figure rises to about two thirds.
Notice that the increase is gradual, not sudden. Numbers rarely jump overnight.
Meanwhile, the share of residents who say they feel lonely falls slightly, and then remains stable.
Of course, we must be careful. A rise in park visits does not prove that parks cause happiness.
It may be that happier people simply visit parks more often. Statisticians call this reverse causation.
Nevertheless, there's good reason to believe that green space helps. Trees reduce noise, lower summer temperatures and give people a place to meet.
For city planners, the challenge is that land is expensive. A park can't be a car park or a block of flats at the same time.
Some cities respond by creating small parks on empty corners, which cost far less than a large one.
For next week, read the article on the course page, and note any graphs that use words like rise, fall, or remain steady.

title: Should Museums Be Free?
focus: Second conditional in argument (If entry were free, ... would ...)

lines.text: Today's motion: museums should be free for everyone. Sara, why do you support it?
Because culture belongs to everyone. If entry were free, more families on low incomes would visit.
I understand the idea, but who pays? If museums lost ticket income, they'd have to cut staff or close galleries.
Governments could cover the cost. Many countries already fund museums, and some have free entry every day.
Taxpayers would then pay for something that not everyone uses. Is that fair?
We pay for roads we don't drive on. Education and culture are public goods.
Fair point. But I'd rather see free entry on certain days, so that museums keep part of their income.
That's a half measure. People who can't afford tickets also can't easily take a day off for a free day.
Perhaps, although free evenings could solve that. In my view, a flexible system works best.
Can you agree on anything?
We agree that access matters. We just differ on how far to go.
Exactly. I'd say it's a question of degree.
A civilised end. Thank you both.

We have the Garden Room, which seats seventy. It costs six hundred pounds for the day, including projector and microphones.
Could you possibly tell me whether refreshments are included?

I see. Would you be able to hold the room for me until Friday? I need to get approval from my director.
Certainly. I can hold it without a deposit until then, but after that I'd have to release it.
That's very kind. One more thing: is there step-free access? One of our speakers uses a wheelchair.
Yes, there's a ramp at the main entrance and a lift to all floors.

title: Run Smart, Stay Fit

lines.text: Welcome to Run Smart. With us is coach Elsa, who is training a group for the spring marathon.
Thanks, Ravi. By this time next month, my group will have been training for four months.
How are they doing?
Well, but a few have picked up injuries. Most of them come from doing too much too soon.
What's the main rule?
Increase your weekly distance slowly. By the end of the programme, they'll have run much longer distances, but it has to be built up gradually.
And what about shoes?
They matter. Worn out shoes can cause knee and ankle problems, so replace them regularly.
What should someone do if they feel pain?
Stop. Running through pain is a bad idea. In a week's time you'll be glad you rested.
Any advice for race day?
Don't try anything new, like new shoes or a new breakfast. You'll be nervous enough already.
Do you run yourself?
Every morning. This time next year, I hope I'll be running my tenth marathon.
